title: [40k] Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Orks
content:
Welcome to 11th Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Orks a tour of the of their weird rules and interactions that I’ve been asked about! If you have an Orks questions you’d like to see answered in a future update to this article please do send them via this form! 

Changelog

  • Published: 2026-09-25

Current Q&A

How does Nazdreg's Kustom Blasta X work?

Confusingly... it's "one" weapon, it has three profiles, you shoot with all of them every time. So it's somewhere between a Combi weapon and just having three weapons. The subtle difference this makes is that because it's "one weapon" it can only have one target, BUT all three profiles are then resolved into that target rather than just one of them.

For anyone coming here from the app who are confused because it shows up in the app as just any other weapon with three profiles would and says you need to pick one profile, open the "unit composition" section of his data sheet to see the note about it

Blasta X weapons has three separate ranged profiles, each of which can be selected to make attacks with.

It was also mentioned in this Warhammer Community post.

Does the Flash Gitz Enhancement “supa-snazz dakka” work with Firing Deck?

Flash Gitz. Credit: 40khamslam.

No. This is probably obvious to plenty of players, but I’m answering it because it’s still a prevalent issue. Some people have even suggested they think the wording of this enhancement is special and that it should work. It’s not.

FLASH GITZ unit only. This unit’s Snazzgun weapons have [Rapid Fire 1].

It’s still that the “units’s weapons” have [Rapid Fire 1]. I’ll admit that it’s not intuitive, but despite how the Firing Deck rule is worded TRANSPORTS don’t actually take the guns your unit has, upgrades and all. That’s not how GW intends Firing Deck to function and has FAQ'd this a few different ways now. TRANSPORTs using the Firing Deck rule are equipped with the same weapons the unit was equipped with, so if you equipped your Ork with a Snazzgun then the TRANSPORT is equipped with a Snazzgun; it’s not THAT same Snazzgun though. Whilst this specific FAQ is about Leader abilities, the logic is the same:

Q: While an attached unit is embarked within a TRANSPORT, do weapons that TRANSPORT shoots with using the Firing Deck ability gain any benefit from any abilities that attached leader has (e.g. a Lieutenant's Tactical Precision ability that grants weapons in it's unit the [LETHAL HITS] ability?

A: No. Firing Deck enables a TRANSPORT to be equipped with a number of weapons equipped by its passengers (Core Rules), but the TRANSPORT itself is not part of that attached unit.

The TRANSPORT is not part of the Flash Gitz unit, so an enhancement that affects the Flash Gitz unit’s weapons does not affect weapons equipped by the TRANSPORT.

How does the Grot Shield Stratagem work?

Grots. Credit: Rockfish

Probably needs a slight wording pass but the stratagem is, at its core, pretty simple.

Your opponent targets an ORKS INFANTRY unit that you have a convenient GRETCHIN unit within 3” of and, until that attacking unit has resolved all of its attacks, any hits that attacking units hits are converted into mortal wounds that hit the GRETCHIN unit until it runs out of models. It could be clearer that it’s not a single hit; the core line to note here is this one:

When a hit roll for that enemy unit’s ranged attacks

Attacks plural.

What about with Lethal or Sustained Hits?

How it interacts with these two rules is a bit less clear though.

Lethal Hits I’m pretty confident are absorbed like any other attack; whilst they do “automatically wound” the target, that specific attack’s whole sequence is ended by the Grot Shield stratagem’s effect, so that automatic wound doesn’t progress any further.

Sustained Hits could probably rile up a few rules lawyers with a half dozen different issues, but erring on the side of keeping things simple: Sustained Hits attacks create more hits, so each one becoming another Mortal Wound for the GRETCHIN unit to take seems the most intuitive interpretation. If you lack sufficient Gretchin to take these mortal wounds, that hit just carries on like any other attack.

Some people that really want to argue that Sustained Hits just makes more hits, but those hits aren’t attacks. Corrode wants me to tell you that anyone arguing that with him, “can eat his ass.”

Infest Warzone but my Gretchin unit had Zodgrod Wortsnagga attached, does Zodgrod return?

This really needs to get an FAQ. Here’s the stratagem in question.

Right now I’d say yes, Zodgrod is returned with the unit, but only in some specific circumstances regarding how they die. The key element here is that the unit is returned at its starting strength. Starting strength is defined specifically in rule 01.02.01:

The number of models a unit contains at the start of the first battle round is its starting strength. The starting strength of an attached unit is the number of models that unit contains at the start of the first battle round.

So if we’re adding a GRETCHIN unit to your army with the same starting strength, that’s only possible if you include Zodgrod. There is a caveat to this, though: The attacks that kill Zodgrod have to be part of resolving the same unit’s attacks that killed the last Gretchin in the unit. The stratagem requires a GRETCHIN unit, which a unit with some Gretchin and Zodgrod would be based on rule 2.1.1:

As well as the keywords listed in each datasheet’s Keywords section, each datasheet name acts as an additional keyword for that unit.

If, however, Zodgrod dies to attacks that targeted a unit that had no Gretchin models remaining, it would not be a GRETCHIN unit and therefore not a valid target for the stratagem. If the unit did have some Gretchin though, I’d suggest the unit remains a GRETCHIN unit long enough for the stratagem to be used, though the rules are a bit fuzzy here. There’s this FAQ about attached unit keywords:

Q: Units have all the keywords of all their models, and attached units have all the keywords of all of their component units. How are destroyed models taken into account for these purposes? A: These statements are only true so long as the models possessing those keywords remain part of the unit; destroyed models do not contribute their keywords to their prior unit.

This does imply that as soon as a model is destroyed the unit no longer has its keywords; but if we follow that line of reasoning to its conclusion then all GRETCHIN units would stop being GRETCHIN units when the last GRETCHIN model died and the stratagem wouldn’t have any eligible targets at all. That seems rather silly to me.

Can a Weird Boy use Da Jump from inside a Transport?

Ork Weirdboy by Craig "MasterSlowPoke" Sniffen

Yes.

Doesn’t even need to be on the board.

Orks Official FAQs

This section will list official GW FAQs when GW shares some.

That's all for this weeks Ruleshammer; if you have some questions you think I should cover in the future though please do send them via this form!  Have any other questions or feedback? title: MTG Reality Fracture is a fantastic Commander set with a terrible precon
content:
Reality Fracture is an incredible set for Commander players, with one important caveat. It has one of the worst precons we've seen in years. That's a blemish on an otherwise clean record, because everywhere else you look, this Magic set is stuffed full of cards to make EDH fans very happy.

There are the new charm cards, ultra-flexible and bound to find a home in plenty of more casual decks. There are both the Samuts: one an incredibly cheap haste enabler, the other making all your instants and sorceries impossible to interact with. There's a new tutor for planeswalkers, a green version of Omniscience, and a blink card every bit as good as Displacer Kitten.

This set is particularly amazing for fans of superfriends strategies, with many, many cards that work well with the planeswalker card type. But, honestly, it's hard to find a popular archetype that didn't receive any fun new toys.

There's Craterclaw Colossus for artifact decks, and the new Avacyn and green enchantment Gardenize for sacrifice decks. Spellslinger players get Geist of Saint Thalia, Landfall players get Hexhaven Invigorator, and Eldrazi players get a brand new Emrakul (and arguably an Omnath too).

And that's only looking at cards for the 99. Because with over 80 legends, Reality Fracture may just have the most new commander options of any Magic multiverse set, even giving Universes Beyond a run for its money. Many of these aren't worth building around but plenty are. The elder sphinxes seem particularly cool, and the Jace deck is absolutely stuffed with fantastic buildarounds.

Which actually segues quite nicely into the other point of this article: ragging on the precon. Multiverse Reforged is a mess, designed - I think - not as a deck to be played, but as a place to squish all the cool alternate universe designs which WotC didn't want to include in the main set with their regular counterparts.

The idea behind Multiverse Reforged is simple. You create cheap token creatures, then use your Jace, Multiverse Architect's ability to essentially polymorph them into an enormous threat. There are no creatures costing less than six mana, ensuring you'll always end up with something big.

It's a great idea in theory, but when we look more closely, the cracks in the mirror are extremely clear. These bomb-y legendary creatures belong in their own decks. They don't share well, and you can forget all about synergy.

For instance, the new Niv-Mizzet is a cracked lifegain payoff… in a deck with next to no lifegain. The Ur-Sphinx cares about sphinxes attacking, but it's the only sphinx in the deck. And Dack Fayden donates creatures while letting you profit off their ETBs, but you have relatively few good ETBs.

The other problem with the deck is that if the creature you cheat out is dealt with, it leaves you in a horrendous spot. Jace, Multiverse Architect takes several turns to tick back up, and the deck lacks enough proliferate or empower Jace abilities to speed up the clock. If your first big creature is dealt with quickly, you may just be out of the game.

I can see what WoC was going for, I think, and I really appreciate that we got an even deeper look at the Echoverse in this precon. It lessens the sting of this amazing idea only spanning a single set, in fact. But the point of a precon is not to distribute cool cards. This deck feels designed to be disassembled.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Gloomspite, by Andy Clark
content:
Image credit: Games Workshop

I’ll just say it from the start: Gloomspite by Andy Clark may be the best Age of Sigmar novel there is. Black Library’s recent re-release of the book gave me a good excuse to read it again and to right the wrong that Tabletop Battles doesn’t yet have a review of it.

The story follows a group of mercenaries, The Swords of Sigmar, as they deliver a message of warning to Draconium, a significant Sigmarite stronghold north of Hammerhal Aqsha. Following the death and damnation of their former co-leader, Varlen, the Swords take his fevered dying words foretelling the destruction of the city as a kind of sacred quest. Varlen’s brother, and now sole leader of the group, Hendrick Saul, is the key proponent of this quest, hoping that helping the city might give some meaning to his brother’s death.

The rest of the Swords are divided on this. Borik, the Kharadron Overlord with a big cannon (which turns out to be a massive 'fuck you' to Chekhov’s gun), is the member of the band who is least convinced by Hendrick’s mission. This is mostly due to the little money there is to be made in the quest. Borik is a faithful Kharadron, bound by the code and its near-religious devotion to profit.

Arkanaut Admiral. Credit: Tiger Millionaire

Romilla, a warrior priestess of Sigmar, is more open to the idea that there is divine guidance behind the dying man’s portents. Maybe even divine prophecy. But there is also the possibility that this could be a trick from the Dark Gods. Varlen was, after all, in the process of transforming into a Chaos Spawn at the time he gave the warning. Romilla is also the matriarchal figure of the group, often the voice of reason and caution to Hendrick.

In the case of Eleonora Van Ghest, engineering genius, Romilla’s matriarchal role is of particular importance. Eleonora lost both of her parents and was kicked out of the engineering guild, left to wonder the streets of Hammerhal completely alone until she was found by Romilla and the other Swords. Eleonora has been having dreams ever since Varlen’s death in which she sees evil eyes in the sky, overlooking the city. As well as being the brains of the operation, providing gadgets, explosives and plans, Eleonora also provides a really healthy example of neurodiversity inclusion in a Warhammer novel. Her character is really nicely handled.

The other Swords complete the archetypes you’d hope to see in any solid fantasy crew. Olt Shev is the barbarian, a heavily tattooed member of the Pyremouth tribe with an affinity to the land, if not to the Sigmarite religion. There is also, of course, a wizard, Bartiman, providing wizened insights and the occasional burst of death magic.  Finally, in order to serve as Legolas to Borik’s Gimli, we need and aelf in there too. Aelyn, the Wanderer (wood elf), completes the group, bringing all the haughtiness and litheness and pointy-eardness you want from an obligatory elven character.

But whilst the group might seem like every other D&D party you’ve ever come across, it is the portrayal of the characters that makes this book so wonderful. Every one of them is rich and sensitively handled. Their interactions are interesting, compelling and believable.  Furthermore, other than Skragrott (more on him later), none of the characters in this book are core AoS characters, none have models, so Clark has a lot of free reign with what he does with them. This leads to a lot of brave choices that you might not otherwise get with more established heroes in AOS lore. They also have no plot armour. When reading a Taliah Vedra book, you can be pretty sure she is going to survive every battle she gets into because her model is still quite new. The Swords don’t have that luxury, so the stakes are higher.

There’s also a great supporting cast in this novel. Captain Helena Morthan, the devout, hard-working, disciplined and underrated commander of the city watch, is shrewd and capable, but not a social climber, instead wanting the best for the city. She knows something is wrong, and reluctantly asks the Swords for help, but is having a hard time trying to convince the city’s leader to devote more resources to the city’s defense.

The city’s leader, Regent Militant Selvador Mathenio Aranesis, is a former war hero now turned much-loved benevolent-but-useless head of state. He keeps his eyes and ears closed to the warning signs of the catastrophe approaching the city, but Helena is determined to remain loyal to him despite this.

There is also a very nicely woven tapestry of other minor characters who come and go throughout: arrogant watchmen, fanatical cultists, terrified civilians, which all serve to give the book a lot of flavour.

Then there’s Skragrott. This book isn’t supposed to be an in-depth psychological study of the Loonking. We see just about enough of him to know just how terrifying he actually is, something you may not realise by looking at his model. That is what is so masterful about this book, it shows us a genuinely creepy, scary and horrifying perspective on grots.

In the past we have been treated to campy, silly goblins in the Warhammer universe. There are some brilliant grot books, Bad Loon Rising is excellent, and the Gloomspite Gitz are still a very viable threat when they show up in books like Gitslayer. But at the same time they’re a little goofy. It’s kind of like Tim Burton’s Batman films, over-the-top, daft, but excellent in their own way.  But Gloomspite serves as the Christopher Nolan Dark Knight reboot.

Most of the book, like in any good horror story, is pure tension building. The goblins don’t even show up until halfway through. Instead, we get claustrophobic storytelling, threats lurking behind every sentence, dread growing with every page. Clark does a great job of giving you just enough, but not too much. He drip-feeds your imagination everything it needs to fill in the sickening gaps. This is the second time I’ve read this book, the first time was closer to when it first came out, and some of the scenes, like when the Bad Moon first ascends into the sky, were still vividly etched into my mind after the first time.

When the grots finally arrive they are portrayed with all of the grim-dark realism you need to fill your therapy sessions for years to come. Things get crazy. Cackling mobs of murderous, black-hooded creatures hacking at legs and feet with rusty shivs. Hulking great troggoths lumbering down ruined abandoned streets making meals out of helpless citizens. Piggy-eyed, snarling balls of teeth hammering against buildings and snapping their jaws around terrified victims. Swarms of insects disemboweling unfortunate villagers. Mushrooms sprouting from human flesh. Minds snapping with terror. Fungal zombies. And malevolent sentient moon glaring down over all of it. Pure nightmare fuel.

Zarbag's Gitz. Credit: SRM

The action is also incredibly well written. I sometimes get a bit lost in fight scenes in Warhammer books. It’s incredibly hard to write truly engaging action scenes. They can get a bit samey. Who’s stabbing who now? But every blow, every fight scene in this book is clearly and engagingly laid out.

And that’s the thing, everything Clark does in this book is done well.  When there’s not a lot happening, which is the case for most of the book, I’m captivated by all the stuff that is left unsaid. When all hell breaks loose and there is madness happening on every page, I’m turning the page with excitement.  And none of this is done at the expense of the characters.  They each have their own arcs which are believable and relatable.

In some way the book is nihilistic and hopeless, but in other ways, in the midst of the clammy dankness of despair, the beauty of what it means to be human (or elf or dwarf) shines all the brighter and there are really excellent portraits of honour, respect and sacrifice. But none of this is done in a cheap or easy way. Borik, for example, maintains his view that none of this was worth it, as they were not getting paid to be there. He doesn’t suddenly change his mind and have his heart warmed by the love of friends, or whatever you might expect to see happen to a greedy curmudgeon in your average Hollywood movie. He is a Kharadron after all, it wouldn’t be faithful to the lore if he suddenly abandoned his code to give in to human sentimentalities. But that doesn’t mean that his arc isn’t still an interesting and redemptive one.

Ultimately, Gloomspite is an opportunity for Andy Clark to show off his quite significant writing chops. He never misses a note. If you haven’t read it yet, I insist you go out and take advantage of its re-release to rectify that.

content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Wings: A quick event spotlight from me up front before I hand you over to Lowest of Men for the event writeups!

Event Spotlight - Paris Wargame Expo

On 17th and 18th October, the French 40K Federation are running the Paris Wargame Expo for the second time, featuring a massive array of events for Games Workshop systems.

Corrode and I went out to the first of these last year, and had an absolute blast, which you can read more about in my post here. This year, the organisers are going even bigger (and at an even larger venue), and the following events are available:

  • 512-player 40K supermajor (running on official GW terrain).
  • 200-player 5v5 40k team tournament.
  • 600-player 2v2 40K
  • A massive 40K Grand Narrative
  • Age of Sigmar singles major
  • Age of Sigmar 2v2
  • Age of Sigmar Narrative.
  • Events for:
    • Underworlds
    • The Old World
    • Blood Bowl
    • Kill Team
    • Horus Heresy
Last year's event in full swing

This year, Games Workshop are also bringing the Hobby Challenge to the PWE. For those who want to focus on the building and painting rather than competitive play, the Hobby Challenge is a really cool way to spend a weekend that I don't think Games Workshop does nearly enough to spotlight, but luckily Cronch has a trip report from the run at the Newport GW open here, so take a look if you're curious.

GW will also be running their event store at the PWE, so for those on the continent who have less frequent access to event exclusives, this is an opportunity to grab them.

There's also goody bags for all participants, and breakfast/lunch included with tournament tickets.

We had a phenomenal time last year, and the event was extremely well run, so if you're looking for a great tournament next month, I highly recommend looking at this, particularly if you're in Europe or the UK (as travel on the Eurostar is dead easy). I am legitimately crushed that I can't go this year due to some unavoidable real-life clashes, so go have fun in my stead!

Tickets and full details are all available on the French Federation Website.

Disclosure: I was offered free tickets/press passes to this event for a promotional post. As above, I am unable to actually go due to some real-life clashes, so we are not receiving any payment for this post, but it is still important to disclose this.

title: Warhammer 40k's new Adeptus Custodes rules make them true tabletop demigods
content:
Following on from the first teasers at the Big Warhammer Autumn Preview, Games Workshop has revealed datasheets for the updated Adeptus Custodes in Warhammer 40,000 - and they're absolute monsters. Fortunately for all the other Warhammer 40k factions, while the Custodes' power level is higher than ever, it seems like their armies will have 33% fewer models than they do right now!

Games Workshop dropped three new datasheets on the Warhammer Community website on Thursday, for the Custodian Guard Sodality, Captain-General Trajann Valoris, and the Telemon Heavy Dreadnought. They build on information that Warhammer spokespeople hinted at during the Preview stream: a single Custodian Guard, from the most basic Sodality squad, has better stats than a Space Marine captain.

Each member of a Custodian Guard Sodality has Toughness 7, Auramite Armor that gives an impressive 2+ save and 4++ invulnerable save, five wounds, and Leadership 5+. An upgraded movement speed of eight inches also make them far better able to close distance for a fight.

The caliber of the bolt rounds in their guardian spears have increased to strength 5, and they've been working on fire frequency with Rapid Fire 2. In melee they swing those shiny sticks with the strength of power fists and six attacks each. Every attack his on a 2+ (natch), and if they or their targets are in range of an objective, they get Sustained Hits 1 thanks to the ability 'Impenetrable Defence'.

While those stats are intimidating, there's one other important piece of the picture - the squad size is shrinking from five models to three. When you compare the effectiveness of the whole squad it has the exact same number of wounds, shoots more shots at close range and fewer at long range, and while its melee attacks are stronger they're not meaningfully better against most tanks or most Space Marines.

They've also lost some useful abilities, particularly a once-per-battle ability to shoot twice in a round, and an ability to re-roll ones to wound (or all wound rolls, when holding an objective). They're definitely more survivable and faster, while their offensive output looks like a sidegrade that leaves them weaker when targeting vehicles and monsters.

Speaking of monsters, Captain-General Trajann Valoris is back and ready to delete things. He gets the same movement speed and toughness upgrade as his warriors, but he's now up to 10 wounds - making him a valid target for the Bring It Down objective. The Eagle's Scream has been sidegraded with an increase in strength and Rapid Fire 2 but a decrease in damage, but the Watcher's Axe is brutal. With Cleave 1 he'll have 10 attacks if he makes contact with an untouched squad of 20 models, and its damage stats go up to S12, AP-3, D4.

His once per battle Moment Shackle has been toned down, now granting him either a 3+ Invulnerable Save or +3A for one phase. But his Captain-General ability has been upgraded in-line with the Primarch Roboute Guilliman - friendly Custodes infantry and jetbikes within 6″ get to re-roll hit rolls and wound rolls of 1. That puts Custodes accuracy up from 83% to 97% (and an average a little bit over 100% if they also have Sustained Hits 1).

Valoris' can still join a unit, though his aura emanates from him specifically, not his bodyguard. With smaller unit sizes that's going to be tricky to apply - it's also hard to think of any threat you might send Valoris and a bodyguard unit into that needs another unit nearby to finish it off.

Last, and absolutely not least, is the Telemon Heavy Dreadnought. With toughness 11 and 14 wounds it's now firmly into battle-tank survivability, especially thanks to the returning 'Guardian Eternal' ability that reduces the damage from attacks that wound it. One key feature for anyone with a resin Telemon is that you can only field it with weapon options you can build from the plastic kit - you can't double up on its ranged weapons.

You may be tempted to take two melee mitts instead, thanks to a new 10″ movement speed. A pair of Caestus Fists grants it seven attacks that hit on 2+, have S14, deal 4 damage, and they're twin-linked. Expect to deal 20 or more damage to any target without an invulnerable save or serious wound mitigation.

Those fists also come with 'Twin Neutronium Cascade-Projectors' built in, flamer weapons that deal a fixed 3 hits and have Blast 1, and are S7 and AP-2 with the twin-linked ability. While it's not mathematically certain that unloading those fists on a squad of 10 guardsmen will kill them all, it's pretty close.

It's clear how you would give the Telemon an anti-infantry ranged loadout, between the Arachnus Storm Cannon - with its masses of shots, Devastating Wounds, and now Sustained Hits 1 - and the Spiculus Bolt Launcher, which has gained Blast 2 on top of a fixed six attacks and an additional point of AP.

The other two guns are odd. With AP-2, D4, and four attacks, the Adrathic Desolator is almost an anti-tank gun, but it's only S10; while the Iliastus Accelerator Culverin's S10, D3, and six attacks when in Rapid Fire Range make it look like a Terminator hunter, except it's AP-1. Both will hurt light vehicles, but the Custodes don't have problems with those.

Even with the recent army-wide power inflation to the Space Marine, and the less extreme but still noticeable tune-ups to the Orks, the Custodes look like absolute beasts. We haven't seen the points yet, but I wouldn't be surprised if armies end up about 40% smaller than before, in model count if not in number of units on the table. That's a great fit for Custodes lore, and will goes even deeper into their current playsty  le that makes every model essential.

If you've got a Custodes army, opinions on these changes, or just want to rave about how much they steal the show every time they get a point of view character in a 40k novel, share your thoughts (or army pictures!) in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: TheChirurgeon's Road Through 2026, Part 40: Testing New Tone Pro Paints
content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I wrote at length about my time at Challengers Cup, playing with the Tabletop Battles team and finishing 2-0-4. That particular journey was a ton of fun and if you missed it, it's worth going back and reading both parts to get a feel for the kind of fun you can get up to at Challengers Cup and 8-man teams events, generally.

Before I get into the meat of this article I have to issue a quick thank you to Games Workshop for providing me with a Sample Paint Set of Warhammer Tone | Pro paints for review purposes. We'll have a formal review on Saturday, but I'm also talking about them today.

I flew back to Houston from Salt Lake City on Monday, spent the night at my house, and then got up Tuesday morning to fly to New York for a work trip. I wouldn't get back home again until Friday. Not as bad as the time I flew directly from Tacoma to New York, but still pretty rough. My son's birthday was also last weekend, which meant I spent most of the weekend running around coordinating a birthday party and playing with Legos as he assembled various kits.

What this meant was that I didn't have the ability to get a game in over the weekend, despite my best intentions. Ok, I didn't really intend to get in a game. I was ready to not play a game for the weekend, and we were snowed in anyways having to write a full 41 articles for the embargo date on Codex: Space Marines. So I spent most of the week helping get content ready for last weekend.

Normally this leads to a pretty light update but this week Games Workshop have been sending out sample paint sets for their new Warhammer Tone Pro line of paints and helpfully told us that we can talk about them as soon as we get them. And as it would turn out, my set showed up last night (Wednesday) at 8pm, suddenly giving me a lot more to talk about and completely changing this week's update.

Warhammer Tone Pro Paints

A set of these dropped on my door last night, giving me a selection of the new paints. Specifically, there was a full set of Blue paints, i.e. #1-5 for Blue Gorkshroom, a trio of Reds (Bloodtoof Red), a trio of greens (Hierotek Green), Black/Grey/White, and one each of Pink, Orange, Yellow, and Bright Green.

There were some issues with the paints - more on those in my big review Saturday - but these struck me as more QC issues than issues with the paints. My big immediate reaction on seeing these paints was "I want to try the pinks to do Emperor's Children." And that was my immediate first go-to here, testing the paint on a pair of Emperor's Children models which I had already primed black.

Loading...

There are basically four things I'm really testing when it comes to these paints:

  1. How's their coverage? This was advertised as excellent, so I want to know how good it is. I want to test lights over darks, and black over everything.
  2. How does it handle being "gooped on" to the model? This is another area where early reviews and preview video have suggested it'll look great.
  3. How does it blend? Can I mix it with other Tone Pro colors and how smooth are the transitions when I layer them up?
  4. How will it look when I start using other paints, especially my older paints?

One key thing about these paints is that they seem to be alcohol-based, and so will not mix. They tend to dry pretty rapidly still - even goopy I was looking at about 15 minutes for them to dry - and they tended to produce a nice finish, though I think you'll still want to use your brush to avoid leaving obvious brush marks or streaks.

Loading...

Coverage on the pink was generally very good. I really felt it needed to coats to get there, but the coats could go on pretty thick and resolved nicely into something that didn't lose detail. They were also incredibly vibrant - the pink is much brighter and pinker than the pink I painted over black with my other models using Pink Horror and Emperor's Children. After I laid down those coats, I ended up using Carroburg crimson to shade the edges and glaze coats of Emperor's Children to blend up to a lighter pink before using Fulgrim Pink to do my edge highlighting and the filigree work.

You can see the difference in saturation: The Tone Pro model is on the left; the older, Pink Horror/EC model is on the right. I'm really happy with how the model turned out and while it's a bit pinker than my older models, I'm OK to keep using this moving forward.

Loading...

After pink came yellow. My best opportunity for doing yellow testing right now is hazard stripes on Iron Warriors so I picked up one of my Mutilators and used him as a test model, painting one coat of Khemri Sands (4) over the black primer. I'd later correct with Blackstone Void (1), which I gotta tell you - it's an amazing black. I previously used Black Legion Contrast paint for doing base rims; I can tell you right now that I will never do that again - Blackstone Void is now the black baserim color of choice.

Loading...

I tested the reds on some Red Corsairs models, using all three tones for highlights and I was impressed with how they seem to self-blend into lower number colors. Normally I do some semi-complicated wet blending with my reds for Red Corsairs armor panels but this time just layering on 2-3-4 of Bloodtoof Red worked remarkably well. I finished it off with Carroburg recesses and Wild Rider Red highlights, but Ideally I can do both of those with Tone Pro paints in the future.

Then there was the white. I don't paint a lot of models white these days but I'll say that the Tone Pro White (Blackstone Void 5) did a fantastic job covering over black. You'd still want two coats - I only used one above - but I'd easily place it on par with my Monument Hobbies white paint or Reaper's Pure White.

That's about all I've done so far. I've only had the paints a few hours but I'm excited to do more with them.

Final Thoughts

That's it for this week. There's more to say about these paints and I'll have a bigger, more detailed review of the Warhammer Tone Pro paints this weekend - stay tuned for that. I have more painting to do to actually play around with the paints and I'm also planning to get in a test game tomorrow against my buddy T, so I'll have more games to talk about next week, with some added sauce as part of that update, so be sure to check back to see what that particular phrase means in this context.

See you Thursday.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Warmachine Faction Focus: Khymaera Shadowflame Shard
content:
Khymaera are among the fastest and hardest hitting factions in MK4 Warmachine.  They have access to a suite of great casters, as well as potent threat extenders.  They also possess the ability to play a wide variety of styles, everything from gun line with Lylyth to a melee focused glass cannon army with Nyxyan and Quick Fangs.  Khymaera also has access to a wide variety of problem-solving tools with universal pathfinder and easy access to guidance.

Changelog

  • Published: 2026-09-24

Strengths

  • Among the fastest factions in Warmachine
  • High Defense

  • Universal Pathfinder or Flight
  • Access to a wide variety of utility tools

Weaknesses

  • Lack of Durability
  • High Point Cost
  • Ranged damage is limited high point models

Army and Playstyle

Leaders

Shyryss

Shyryss is the squishiest of the Khymaera casters with only 14 ARM and 15 Boxes; as a result, she can die to blasters more than any other leader.  With that limitation in mind, she is one of my go two casters.  She has the same speed as other Quick Fnags, making her among the faster casters in the game at SPD 7. She also has the ability to jump for free letting her move 12” before taking her combat action.  Sadly, she does not have a melee weapon so she cannot charge.  Lastly she has Repo 3” letting her move to safety after contributing.  She also brings field marshal prowl, giving stealth to her battle group when they have concealment.

Shyryss’s individual contribution with her gun is amazing.  It is a RAT 7, RNG8, POW10 gun - pretty weak at first glance.  There are several factors that turn it around, the first of which is ROF 3.  This lets her leverage multiple of her shot types. Second, all her thrown daggers have witchmark – not as a shot type, they just have witchmark.  Most leaders with multiple shot types must use a shot just to apply witchmark, Shyryss does it for free.  On top of that she has three different shot types; Shadowbind (Not crit shadowbind), Poison (extra damage dice against living) and Snipe (+3 RNG).

Credit - Trish Ross

Her spell list is also fantastic.  Everyone one of her spells can be a defining spell for a caster.  First distraction, -2 DEF, -2 MAT, and the target cannot make ranged attacks.  This spell shuts down units, and if you are aggressive enough, some casters. (Sorry Caine, no guns for you).  Mirage allows for a 2” place during the control phase – it can be used as a basic threat extender, or as a way to allow for a unit to reposition prior to charging, letting them position around a building or into a forest.  Banishing Ward protects high value targets from enemy spells or upkeeps. Hand of Destruction is signs and portents for her battle group, always useful.  Finally she has Host of Shadows - which makes her battlegroup ghostly – letting them pass through terrain.  A huge deal for models that struggle with impassible terrain like Triks.

Shyryss feat is -3 SPD on charges and slams against models in her control range, concealment (procc'ing prowl on her battle group) and dodge.  The -3 SPD on charges can be punishing – in many ways it is equivalent to +3 SPD when determining which player will get the alpha strike.  An important perk to note, only your models need to be in your control range, not the enemies.  A savvy opponent will notice that her feat does not apply trample power attacks – opponents can trample their full distance and start buying attacks.  Usually this is not a good idea, but at times it is so keep that option in mind.

When trying to shut down a key warbeast my standard procedure is move within 8” and throw a shadowbind shot at a model.  I will typically boost to hit with this shot but not boost damage.  I will then cast Hand of Destruction (auto hitting because of witchmark).  I will then throw two more poison daggers boosting damage.  Even against ARM18 these shoots typically do about 8 damage each, with potential for some really nasty spikes. Once that is done Shyryss will reposition backwards 3”, and commonly feat while the rest of your army moves forward and does work.

Kyrrax

Kyrrax’s defining trait is Alpha Hunter – an ability that gives his entire battlegroup +2 MAT and SPD.  It is triggered off  him killing a model, as well providing free runs or charges to entire battlegroup.  That ability alone is something you can build a list around.  Kyrrax will typically leverage an arc node in order to cast Battering Ram at a weak single wound infantry model just to trigger Alpha Hunter.  He is fairly tanky at 13 DEF, 20 ARM (counting the shield), so he is prepared to position further forward than most casters.  That is required if he is going to get any value out of Vortex of Destruction – which gives boosted damage rolls against enemies in his melee range.

While Alpha Hunter encourages players to build a beast heavy list, his feat encourages the opposite.  It provides friendly faction warrior models +2 to hit.  Additionally, when a model in his control range destroys or removes from play an enemy model, a warrior model in his control range can make a 2” advance followed by an attack.

Nyxyan

Nyxyan, while one of my favorite casters in Khymaera, is in a bit of an odd state.  Her kit is focused on supporting infantry, while also being ARC 8 -- meaning she needs multiple beasts to provide her with the fury she needs to cast spells.

She brings Dash, mix that with Hunters Mark from a Vypex and infantry that originally threatened 11” now threaten 14” – which will out threats most other units.  She also has Breath Stealer, a -2 SPD, -2 DEF debuff.  It only costs 2, mixed with her ARC of 8 means she can cast it twice boosting to hit both times.  A -2 DEF debuff is not to be underestimated.

Credit - Trish Ross - Nyxyan

Her feat, which only affects friendly faction warrior models, lets them share the benefits of Prey for a +2 to Hit and +2 to damage (and also change Prey's target). Interestingly, the only part of her feat that is restricted to her control range is the selection of a new Prey target, letting her gain the benefit all over the field.

She also has Revelations of the Outer Darkness, letting her cast a spell when a friendly warrior model is killed while within 12” of her.  I find the three most useful spells to cast with Revelations of the Outer Darkness are: Blackest Night, for a -1 on enemy attack rolls while within 10” of her, Admonition creating a new challenge for an enemy to crack, or Caustic Mist from Aklyss disrupting my opponents line of sight mid turn for forcing them to replan their turn.

Lastly, Nyxyan is sitting on a strangely effective spell assassination.  Using her feat and blessing of the gods for an extra focus, Nyxyan is able to cast Howling Flames 3 times, putting out AAT 9 POW 15 magic sprays.  Very few things in the game are able to negate magical sprays, and if a caster is low on resources the assassination is there for the taking.

Rassyk

Rassyk brings an interesting toolkit to Khymaera.  He has significant personal output with a MAT 8, POW 17 weapon and access to flashing blade meaning he can kill a heavy on his own if he wants to.  His battle plans allow him to build a defensive brick combining battle formation and mortal fear from Ryvyn for an effective +4 ARM swing.

His feat provides reposition 3” along with defensive strike.  This can be combined with models like the Drakyon which have potent on hit effects that can shut down opponents charges.  If faced with a mountain of tough models, Deathbringers gives grievous wounds to all the melee attacks of members of his battle group.  Warpath allows for a cohort model in his battle group to move 3” outside of activation working as a threat extender, a reposition move, or a laundry list of other tricks.  Lastly Disintegration provides some damage output while also acting as an ARM debuff opening the door for further damage.

Lylyth

Lylyth is the meta leader for Khymeara and is a staple in a lot of pairs.  She brings a strong gun with option of 3 POW 14 shots, or a single Armor Piercing POW 10 shot with Crit Stagger.  Stagger causes the model hit to loose ALL of it’s initial attacks.  On a colossal this can be 7+ attacks – crippling players plans.  Players will lean on her to crit stagger key enemy pieces which becomes very reliable with Deadeye adding an additional dice, boosting, and puppet strings for a re-roll of the crit doesn’t connect.  The down side of that tactic is she will typically not one shot the key piece meaning run and gun won’t trigger.  Lylyth players will then play careful reconnaissance on her to allow her to reposition 3” back to safety.

Deadeye can be used as a RAT fixer for any model in the faction, making normally unreliable pieces very effective.  While beasts are the traditional target, Quick Fang Masters throwing blind bombs have ruined more than one players day.  (See the bit on the quickfang master lateron)  Slipstream is a powerful threat extender that does not require rolling to hit like hunters mark does.  Lastly Silence of Death boosts the power of any unit it is cast on.

In terms of playstyle, Lylyth could best be described as sandpaper.  Her army will move up, remove a layer of models at the front, before triggering run and gun and moving back to safety.  Her feat is typically used to disrupt your opponents scenario position.  Traditionally gunlines like Lylyth typically runs struggle on scenario but Lylyth’s feat solves this problem.

Vallyx

Vallyx brings a wonderful bucket of tools to build around.  His feat, Blood Moon, makes every attack against enemies in his control range a critical hit.  Automatically critically hitting enemies opens some potent doors.  First, he can trigger his own weapons crit effects to automatically knockdown enemies that he charges, it also opens the door on two other key pieces in Khymaera.  Both the Trik and the Hydrix both have heads that are Crit Armor Piercing.  Armor Piercing cuts an opponent’s base ARM in half.  The Trik will swing at dice plus 9 in most case, with the Hydrix swinging at dice plus 7.  Few things can survive 4 or more attacks hitting that hard.

Credit - Trish Ross - Vallyx

Vallyx has a base 12” melee threat, but that can be extended 3” with vanish.  If you bring a hunters mark Vypex, that threat can be extended to 17”.  That alone allows Vallyx to bully the board.  His two weapons are both weapon master and carry major crit effects – knockdown and weaken respectively – which when combined with his feat allow him to kill the majority of leaders in Warmachine.  The final major part of Vallyx kit is Well of Hate, providing Murderous to models in his battle group (including himself) letting his army much away at high defense enemies.

Beasts

Aklyss

Aklyss brings two key tools.  First, Master of Ruin, decreasing the ARM of all OTHER models within 5” (including your own!).  The ARM debuff is then able to be heavily leveraged by the rest of the army.  The other key tool Aklyss brings is Caustic Mist.  This animus places a 3” cloud within his control range.  When combined with castings from your leader, this allows a ~9” cloud wall to be placed – causing a massive headache for many opponents.  If you leverage terrain, you can often block between half and a third of the board.

Credit - Trish Ross

Drakyon

The Drakyon the most durable beast in Khymaera per point; its ARM 19 and unyielding animus easily bring it up to ARM 21.  The flip side is it only POW 15 and POW 13 on its weapons – sure the POW 13 will usually gain the benefit of Trash since the Gore attack knocks models over, but the equivalent of POW 16.5 is nothing to write home about.  Smite on the Gore attack can be used in cute ways such as defensive strikes under Rassyks feat – but it struggles to find a home in many lists.

Hydrix

The Hydrix is one of the most dynamic beasts in Warmachine.  It can be built in a wide variety of ways.  It can be built as a traditional melee beatstick with the Toothy Maw head.  It can also be built as a gun beast leveraging the Flame Spitter head, and the Venom spitter heads on the smaller heads.  It can also be built for a more supporting role with the Diviner head to hand out Future Sight, letting you boost after rolling, then two Venom Spitter heads to contribute from safety.  If paired with Vallyx one head will usually be dedicated to the crit armor piercing head – which when combined with his feat makes it one of the hardest hitting tools in the game.

Credit - Trish Ross

Shadow Seraph

While the jury is still out on the Shadow Seraph, signs right now point to it being underpowered.  It boasts one incredibly powerful attack (POW 14 Armor Piercing is amazing), but otherwise it is pillow fisted with all followup attacks coming in at POW 15.  Coming in at 21 points, a heavy that can not kill most other heavies struggles to find a role in most lists.  The Shadow Seraph’s gimmick is the ability to cast one of it’s 3!!!! animi after being hit.  All of these animi increase it’s defense which in theory make the Shadow Seraph very challenging to deal with.  Unfortunately there are quite a few tools that just shut it down.  Things like silence, mage static, or even casting guidance on the attacking model cripple the Shadow Seraphs defensive tech leaving you with a beast that struggles to deliver value.  The flip side is, if your opponent does not have the tools to counter the Shadow Seraph it can be nigh unkillable.  Most of the games top lists have the right tools to shut it down, so it struggles to find a place.

Skylla

Skylla is the character Hydrix in Khymaera.  She boasts two unique things.  First, Rejuvenating Miasma – which is a cloud that heals friendly models within 3” of her.  This can be combined with Shyryss to trigger field marshal prowl providing stealth all the times.  Skylla’s other tool is Transfiguration on her spray and Vorpal Maw.  These attacks allow you to return grunts to various units when she kills enemy models – those returned models then healed by Rejuvenation Miasma assuming they activate after Skylla.

Trikhymaerax

The Trikhymaerax, or Trik is a beast stick of a beast.  Coming in a Def 11 ARM 19 with Rapid healing, it is deceptively durable.  Its defense is just high enough that opponents will miss with some attacks given the volume of attacks required to kill it.  Rapid healing almost always being in place makes it pseudo-ARM 21 since it will heal an average of two points of damage from every damaging attack.  As a colossal it is immune to the Anti Heal aspect of Torment and Grievous Wounds, so its main fears are Entropic Force or Mortality.

There are many different loadouts for the Trikhymaerax, but the staple upgrade is the Arcane Negation tail.  The negation tail allows you to force the Trikhymaerax to negate a spell targeting it, or a model within 3”.  This allows you to shut down spells that would otherwise cripple a colossal such as Mortality, Stranglehold, Deadweight, or Crippling Grasp.

When running with Vallyx, the armor piercing head is acceptable, but if run with another leader the Trik needs either the Gulper head or the Arcane Many-Eyed Head in for damage output.  The Many-Eyed head swings at POW 19, enough to destroy most non-buffed targets, and because of Purgation, it ends up hitting buffed targets even harder.  The downside of the Purgation head is you lose the Eyeless head, which, while expensive, gives you access to two powerful tools.  First, Force wall as an Animus often used to provide +2 Def and blast resist to Quick Fangs or the Shades makes the staggeringly durable.  The Trik itself is also a great target for Force Wall.  Force Wall will shift it from  DEF 11 to DEF 13, a critical swing in defense.  The Eyeless head also offers a slam ranged attack.  Crucially, the slam attack lets you roll the distance slammed, then choose the direction the model will move.  That knowledge allows for pinpoint shenanigans.

In terms of ranged weapons, it is generally a choice between more effective shots, or weapons with pistol if you plan on brawling with your Trik.  Both are solid choices.

Vypex

Vypex tend to fall into two categories.  The first is the 10 point version with Asp/Hunter’s Mark/Cleavers.  This version is basically just there to provide hunter’s mark.  10 points is pricey for it, but getting the alpha strike off is often a key factor in victory.  If points are available the Cleavers will usually be upgraded to Impalers to shift the Vypex from just being a hunters mark tool, to a solid melee piece.  The downside of the Vypex is at only ARM 16 and 26 boxes, you are paying the same points as a heavy for the defensive stats of a light.  Players will also occasionally run the Viper head, to attempt to leverage Side Step and it’s 3 initial attacks to Pac-man through troops.

Credit - Trish Ross - Warmachine Vypex

Wyvern

Clocking it at 19 points a Wyvern is a pricy beast.  It brings solid damage output at POW 18 base.  The Wyvern natively threatens 13”; however, that is only with the low POW tail.  Truth be told is only threatens 12”.  Combined with Bellighul, and the Wyvern his hitting at POW 20, enough to remove most heavies.  It’s animus, Draconic Aura increases the POW of all fire damage rolls by 2, while also preventing continuous fire from expiring.  It’s potent if built around.  The Wyvern’s spray, Nyxyan, Wyrmspine Cinderbacks, and Trik all love the effect.  Frustratingly, the Wyvern’s spray does not have pistol, limiting its effectiveness on a beast that needs to be in melee to earn its keep.

Credit Trish Ross

Solos

Incarnate Conjuror

Incarnate Conjurors are generally considered more cute than good, but they can still be fun.  They bring an aura of -2 to hit for enemy models that are on fire.  This, when combined with a Wyvern can create some interesting situations.  Additionally, the Conjuror can cast Firestarter making a friendly faction models attacks always do continuous fire.  This can be combined with AoE attacks to set a broad swath of your opponent’s force on fire.

Credit - Trish Ross - With such an amazing model I wish the Incarnate Conjuror were good

Pythia

Pythia is a staple in Khymaera lists.  She brings a free upkeep, as well as being an expendable arc node.  While she no longer has auto hit on her weapon, it is often worth charging her to dispel key enemy spells increasing armor.  She is then able to reposition 3” out of melee, leaving her free to function as a channeler.

Regulus

Regulus is a high defense contesting piece.  Espionage, while powerful, will rarely be impactful since you must be quite far forward to successfully trigger it.  He can be frustrating to kill, but boosted attacks will still do it.  Currently most players leave him on the shelf.

Ryvyn

Ryvyn brings two key things to Khymaera.  The first is mortal fear, making all living enemy models within 8” suffer -2 to damage rolls.  A key thing to note, this is not just melee, but also ranged attacks and spells.  Ryvyn also has a weapon master thresher attack – in the right position this attack can be devastating.  He can move forward 6”, jump another 5”, then thresher everything within 2” of him.

Credit - Trish Ross - Talk about a model with style

Shadowmancer Scion

The Shadowmancer Scion is brought for one reason – puppet strings.  If you absolutely need an ability to go off, puppet strings lets you reroll that result.  Commonly a player will put puppet strings on a Vypex before attempting to caster hunters mark, or Lylyth uses puppet strings to ensure she triggers crit stagger on her full draw attack.

The Scion is not a one trick pony and can be used for other aspects – but they are situation rather than central.  Grip of Shadows boosts increases the odds of spells hitting key targets which Nyxyan and Wyrmspine Shadowmancer’s appreciate.  DEF 15 with stealth is also a durable defensive stat line.  Lastly, if the opportunity arises, the Scion can charge in and utilize its two blessed attacks to attempt to trigger battle wizard then cast Stygian Abyss to put some damage out.  Its rarely plan A, but it is a solid plan B – well, maybe plan C.

Spinner

The Spinner is the only 2 point solo in Khymaera and is often used to fill in leftover points.  The Spinner can be used to cast Grim Returns to return a friendly trooper model.  This will most often be used on Incarnate Knights since they are the most durable warriors Khymaera has access to. The other interesting aspect of the Spinner is the Acid Bomb – notably the fact that the blast is POW 12/10.  The high strength of the blast damage allows you to remove obnoxious high DEF models without needing to succeed the roll to hit.

Wraithwing Paragon

The Wraithwing paragon is the premier anti shooting tech in Khymaera.  The Paragon offers blast resistance and enemies suffer -3” RNG if they are targeting friendly models within 3”.  The -3” range aspect is crucial for keeping our beasts and high value pieces safe.  A weapon going from RNG 14 to RNG 11 means if you are getting shot, you can charge them.  The blast resistance aspect is crucial for keeping Quick Fangs alive.  Their ARM 12 will die in droves even to POW 7 blasts, but the Paragon keeps them safe.

The Paragon’s personal damage output is unreliable.  MAT 7, POW 15 with crit decapitation is pretty potent, but famously it will always miss – it’s a meme at this point.  When it does hit, it can hit like a ton of bricks, and sprint away to continue to add value.

Credit - Trish Ross - Wraithwing Paragon - Not to be confused with a beast

Bellighul

Bellighul is technically a mercenary, but he only works for one faction - Khymaera.  He brings a handful of tools, but the reason he is taken is Enrage.  It is a +2 damage swing on every attack on a key model makes.  This can be used to crank a Trik or a Wyvern up to 11 in terms of damage.

Credit - Trish Ross

Units

Incarnate Knights

Incarnate Knights are unique within Khymaera, they are the only unit in the faction that can really take a beating.  They struggle in terms of damage output only having 3 attacks, but they make up for it by having ARM 20 (counting +2 for Battle Driven) and 30 boxes across all 3 of them.  This puts their durability on par with most heavies.  They are commonly run to contest enemy objectives or to jam an opponent.  If you are running Kyrrax they are the ideal Dauntless Resolve target.  That will take them to ARM 23, tough, and they natively have steady meaning they are quite a tough thorn to remove.

Quick Fang Stalkers

Quick Fang Stalkers are my single favorite unit in Khymaera.  They threaten 11” base, but with access to hunter’s mark, or another tool like slipstream or dash it can easy move to 13” to 15”.  They also possess Acrobatics combined with pathfinder which basically means they ignore half the rules in the game.  Acrobatics lets them move over models, but just as importantly it ignores intervening models when declaring a charge target.  This means you can charge models behind a jamming wall with no trouble.  They also have ambush and advanced deploy letting them get to key places fast.

They pack two attacks, but I would say about 60% of the time, I end up using the combo strike.  Pow 13 is enough to start to apply damage to ARM 19 on the charge.  The choice between combo strikes or single swing usually comes down to the opponents stat line.  If the target only has one wound and are living, 99% of the time, you want single swings.  Anatomical Precision means that you no longer even have to roll for damage and will simply remove the models on hit.  Anatomical Prevision also prevents tough regardless of the targets living or unliving state.  With infantry units 98% (source – trust me bro) of the time you want to charge with infantry models, Anatomical Precision means you are often part of the 2%.  If the target unit has set defense, you will often NOT want to charge.  The extra damage die isn’t important and suffering -2 on to hit rolls isn’t worth it.  If you don’t need the speed – don’t charge.

Credit - Trish Ross - Quickfang Stalkers approach a Cryx Stalker.

The final amazing thing about Quick Fang Stalkers is their resilience.  They are like cockroaches.  DEF 14 is a break point, 5 models with DEF 14 who have charged in and positioned as spread out as possible become very hard for a lot of players to deal with.  Mix in stealth and there are few things that can reliably remove them.  The two things that DO terrify Stalkers are blasts, which just pick them up in droves, and E-leaps.  Avoid those two things and your Quick Fangs will have long happy lives.

Quick Fang Wind Strikers

Quick Fang Wind Strikers are the premier ambush unit in the army.  They can ambush in and move to contest key scenario elements while also being Def 14 and stealth.  They have crit shadow bind on their shots which can be useful in niche cases.  When used with Vallyx that niche case becomes something you can plan around, shadow binding cavalry and other models that don’t have easy access to shake.  Wind Strikers also do an automatic D3 points of damage to the target completely bypassing armor.  This is useful into High ARM single wound infantry.  Other ideal targets are Kithguard Guard Towers, a 5 man unit has a very solid chance of removing one.  The other thing to keep in mind is that the D3 damage is bypasses ancient shroud on models like Vorony in Old Umbry and Blood Sirens in Fane of Nyrro letting the Wind Strikers cripple pieces that usually take way more resources to remove.

Shades

The Shades deserve an entire article on their own.  Their ability to scalpel out key pieces is second to none. Their speed and Unpredictable Movement, letting them place within 4" instead of 2", allows for some insane placement tricks.  Additionally, Fortune Hunter, gives them an additional dice to hit and damage against characters makes them a serious assassination threat at all times.  One not so direct trick is to move forward, and place the moving shade ~11” from a scenario element.  From there, you place a second shade 4” away towards that element.  The Shades then reposition 3", with the forward Shade moving to contest, and the originally placed model moving further away into safety.  This maneuver lets you contest with one frustrating to deal with model at a time.

Credit - Trish Ross

Talon Death Dealers

Talon Death Dealers are the second most durable unit it Khymeara. ARM 15 with unyielding and 8 boxes is still not that durable. They are one of the few MAT 7 units in Khymeara letting them operate relatively support free. Their POW 13 finisher attacks let them hit harder than most units, charging into a damaged ARM 19 model, a unit of them will do an average of 24 points of damage. I have found them most useful as a second wave unit, letting other units like Quick Fang stalkers charge in first and inflict a little damage before the Death Dealers come though as second wave – this ensure that Finisher is always active.

Credit - Trish Ross

Talon Lashers

Talon Lashers bring a unique state line, DEF 14 ARM 14 and 8 boxes. The DEF 14 is a major trait for survivability.  In a world where MAT 6 is standard, DEF 14 can be a hurdle. They also bring a unique combination of offensive traits. RNG 3 on melee weapons combined with reposition lets the unit charge in, place 2 inches away, reposition, then engage a line of models ~18.5 inches long.  They can also leverage their two attacks in an attempt trigger crit knockdown.  They are also able to drag key enemy models out of position, opening doors for others to charge in and position more advantageously.

Credit - Trish Ross - Talon Lashers

Wyrmspine Cinderbacks

Cinderbacks have been shunned for the most of the last year but folks are starting to come around to them.  8 points for three blasts helps a lot in a world where there are lots of cheap infantry running around.  When combined with either Lylyth for dead eye, or Nyxyan for prey, they become very consistent.  When they throw their bombs they generate a cloud where they were standing which can be quite useful blocking line of sight to models behind them – the big downside is that the Cinderbacks will still be on the cloud after throwing their bombs and Khymaera does not have an easy way to reposition the unit back – only Rassyk’s feat will do that.

Wyrmspine Shadowmancers

Wyrmspine Shadowmancers are among the first units added to most Khymaera armies. They bring two key traits - Guidance and Condition.  Guidance offers units eyeless sight to target model.  As much as our opponents assume everything in Khymaera has eyeless sight, only two models actually have it. Having eyeless sight on a stick is almost as good. The other utility aspect of the Wyrmspine Shadowmancers is condition, removing excess fury allows for Khymaera players to run more beasts than they otherwise would. (It also lets you put extra fury on a beast in the event that you didn’t put enough on them during their activation – a mistake I have NEVER made) Lastly they have access to Flesh Eater, a pow 10 arcane attack. It is almost never used, usually when you are desperate to kill a random contesting model.

Credit - Trish Ross - Khymaera Wyrmspine Shadowmancers

Quick Fang Master

The Quick Fang Master is the only attachment in Khymaera.  It clocks in at 3 points, which is quite steep for an attachment; however, they bring a staggering amount of utility. Most often taken with Quick Fang Stalkers their key tool is their Blight Bomb.  The Blight Bomb has pistol and can be used in melee and will frequently be the first attack made as part of a charge.  The two attack types that are used most are Rust, reducing the ARM of a key construct by -2.  This can be stacked with other debuffs Khymaera have access to in order to make Quick Fang Stalkers hit well above their weight class.  The other useful option is Black Oil, which blinds the target and the closest model with 1”.  This brings a -4 def swing that will cripple most targets.  The grenade is AoE 1, so if you are sloppy you can hit your own models with the blast.  It also opens another opportunity.  If your opponent has placed a low DEF model within 1” of a high def model, lob the grenade at the low defense model while positioning your models such that the AoE will hit the high DEF true target.

Sample List

This is JVM's most recent Lylyth list.  He is the top ranked Khymaera player, and has been for quite some time.  Lylyth is also Khymaera's most popular leader by a long ways and is present in the overwhelming majority of pairs.

JVM's Lylyth List

Khymaera - Shadowflame Shard

Grand Melee - 100 pts

Lylyth, the Raven Vengeance

14 Hydrix 1

  • 4 CENTRAL HEAD - Toothy Maw
  • 4 SMALLER HEAD - Venom Spitter
  • 4 SMALLER HEAD - Venom Spitter
  • 2 DORSAL FEATURE - Spineback

13 Hydrix 2

  • 3 CENTRAL HEAD - Diviner
  • 4 SMALLER HEAD - Venom Spitter
  • 4 SMALLER HEAD - Venom Spitter
  • 2 DORSAL FEATURE - Spineback

19 Wyvern

4 Bellighul, Master of Pain

3 Pythia

3 Shadowmancer Scion

5 Wraithwing Paragon

11 Incarnate Knights

7 Quick Fang Stalkers

9 Shades

8 Wyrmspine Cinderbacks

4 Wyrmspine Shadowmancers

PC COMMAND CARD

  • Bite and Hold
  • Blessings of the Gods
  • Careful Reconnaissance
  • Duck And Cover!
  • Put The Fires Out

TOTAL POINTS 100/100

List Building with Khymaera

List building starts with a unit of Wyrmspine Shadowmancers then expands from there.  Most of the leaders in Khymaera are looking for a mix of beasts and infantry.  Each leader supports different aspects of the army and needs to be built accordingly.

Kyrrax: Mixed force to leverage his feat and alpha hunter.

Lylyth: Leans heavily into ranged beasts to maximize the power of run and gun.

Nyxyan: Her entire kit supports units.

Rassyk: Lists are built to be durable and leverage defensive strike.

Shyryss: Leans into a combined arms play style while shutting down charges.

Vallyx: Leans into beasts, particularly those with strong crit effects.

What to Watch Out For

The Shades and other insanely fast assassination attempts.  The Shades alone open so many doors with what they can do with Ricochet.  Units like Quick Fang Stalkers combined with speed buffs allow for units to get where most players did not expect them.  Finally, Lylyth, like in the last three editions of Warmachine, is always sitting on a ranged assassination if you don’t respect it.

Final Thoughts

Khymaera bring a wonderful mixtures of playstyles to the game.  They are able to run a melee focused army, a gunline, or a combined arms playstyle.  They have a wonderful selection of tools that let them solve problems.

title: Are Pokémon scalpers actually 'crashing out' over 30th Celebration?
content:
If I had to choose one word to sum up the feeling in the Pokémon community right now, it would be Schadenfreude - the joy that comes from learning about another person's misfortune, suffering, or failure. That might seem like cruelty from fans of a game about forging bonds with cartoon critters, but the misfortune that everyone is celebrating here is that of scalpers and resellers, who (apparently) were burned hard by 30th Celebration.

Scalpers did their usual nefarious thing with this set, buying up as many products as they possibly could from stores, with the plan to sell them on later to Pokémon fans desperate for their cardboard fix. But The Pokémon Company pulled out all the stops and created more product than usual for the anniversary set, tanking their value on the secondary market.

These packs are also believed to have exceptionally good pull rates, with rarer cards appearing way more often than usual, making even the best chase cards from 30th Celebration far less pricey than past sets. Scalpers' dreams of profiting big from this set have gone up in flames. Ding dong, the witch is dead!

That's the story anyhow, and there have been some spectacular rants from Discord servers and Reddit doing the rounds all over social media. One particularly infamous example by a user named Paul claims that TPC is "hurting the people that actually ensure their business makes money" and that they need to buy it all up themselves to save "countless small business owners like myself". Hilarious!

Everyone, from mainstream news sites to the biggest YouTubers, is seizing on this story because it's good content and everyone really wants it to be true, but I'm not convinced by this narrative. A few unconfirmed social media posts are not evidence that the bulk of scalpers have lost money over this release, and in fact I reckon that most will probably make their bucks back in the end.

After all, it's not as though retail stores are replete with spare 30th Celebration ETBs; they are still selling out very swiftly. And right now in fact you can find these boxes selling on eBay for three times the retail price. Hardly something for scalpers to cry about.

Singles do seem to be a lot lower in price than usual, with many falling after release and the 'Future Rare' cards in particular barely beating $100 (I'm not shocked, they're kind of hideous). But even that ignores plenty of other hits in the set, from big classic collection cards like Lugia, to the RGB Mews that are selling for thousands of dollars.

And let's be honest, even if it was true that scalpers had lost big on 30th Celebration, unless this happened for multiple Pokémon sets in a row, it wouldn't dissuade those trying to make money from it. Sorry to rain on your parade, everyone, but Pokémon's true evil team isn't beaten yet.

title: Liked the Resident Evil movie? Here's a new RPG you'll be dying to try
content:
Confession time - I haven't seen Resident Evil in cinemas yet. It's on my to-do list! I'm a sucker for third person horror games, and all the reviews suggest it's a genuine love-letter on the genre, complete with weird key puzzles, dutch camera angles, and an implacable nemesis enemy. And over in tabletop land I've found an RPG that looks equally dedicated to capturing those survival horror vibes: Ink Ribbon.

Ink Ribbon is an upcoming game from Emmet Byrne, lately of Cubicle 7, author of excellent tabletop RPGs Age of Sigmar: Soulbound and the D&D-like Broken Weave, now founder of the studio Old Oak Games. My colleague Gab spotted Ink Ribbon back in July, and on Tuesday Old Oak Games launched a crowdfunding campaign on Backerkit to make it a reality.

Having looked at the offer on Backerkit, I'm not surprised - it's advertising just about every feature that a survival horror fan could want. That starts with the setting. The game takes place in the final hours of Sparrow City, overrun by zombies and even worse bioweapon monsters. Players take on the role of groups of survivors doing their best to make it out alive.

The campaign gives this common enough setup an interesting twist with legacy mechanics. Rather than play as a single group of survivors for multiple sessions, you'll take on the role of multiple groups, each playing through roughly the same span of time but in different parts of the city.

The game comes with a sizeable map - which looks like it was torn straight out of Silent Hill 2 - and you'll record where and when major events happen, from buildings being explored to bridges collapsing. In later sessions, you'll hear an explosion that you caused in another session, or enter the wreckage of a previous disaster from a different direction. You may even be able to loot your old character's corpse - assuming they aren't already up and moving around.

I think that's a promising structure for a survival horror game. Done right you'll get to experience a city-wide catastrophe, a sense of development and progression, and the characters in any given adventure can die without it making the campaign grind to a halt.

There are lots of other survival horror tropes worked into the game design. You'll have a grid based inventory, and the deluxe version of the game comes with tokens for each item so you can play inventory Tetris. Weapons, ammo, and health items are in short supply, but there is a crafting system that lets you press bullets and mix medicinal plants from raw ingredients. There are even safe rooms that monsters can't go into, simply "cause those are the rules".

In one last touch that will hit nostalgic survival horror fans hard, the rules, monster guide, and scenarios are broken up into multiple small pamphlets which look to be about the same size and shape as the game manual in a PS2 disc case. Both the standard and deluxe versions of the game are packaged tidily into a box, and I have to wonder if Byrne intends to translate this for the Japanese market where all-in-a-box RPGs are de rigeur.

The campaign is off to a roaring start, and an extra scenario and extra monster guide have already been unlocked through stretch goals. As ever with crowdfunding, take a good hard look at your pile of potential before backing. You've got until 8pm PDT / 11pm EDT on October 22 (4am BST on October 23) to get involved.

Survival horror TTRPGs are a rare beast (as opposed to RPGs with horror themes, which are pretty common), with All Flesh Must Be Eaten probably the earliest big forebear of the genre. If you've got memorable table tales from horrific RPG encounters, I'd love to hear them in the Wargamer Discord community.
